item.title: Psychological Benefits of Grand Ultimate Fist with Aging
item.description:
Mindfulness

Psychological Benefits of Grand Ultimate Fist with Aging

Considerable research shows that Tai Chi Chuan training improves health.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Holistic, mindfully integrated practices can benefit health across the lifespan.
  • Effects of Tai Chi Chuan have been assessed in many studies in older adults.
  • Traditional martial arts like Tai Chi Chuan improve many aspects of psychological health in older adults.

Traditional martial arts training is often cited as a mindful mind-body practice that can improve and maintain health. I often write about applications and implications of new research studies. Importantly, summary and review papers aggregate data across studies and time, allowing for estimates of replication and overall effects.

Let's make a map!

Recently, researchers Lissandra Zanovelo Fogaça, Mariana Cabral Schveitzer, Arthur Ferreira, Andreia do Carmo Feitosa, Michael Pratt, Caio Fábio Schlechta Portella, Ricardo Ghelman, and Luiz Roberto Ramos in Sao Paolo, Brazil and San Diego, USA, surveyed the scientific literature on health outcomes in older adults after Tai Chi Chuan (or Grand Ultimate Fist) training. Their objective was to assess, synthesise, organize, and create an "evidence map" that summarizes what is scientifically known, what the quality of evidence shows, and what remains to be better explored about the health benefits of Tai Chi Chuan training across the lifespan.

Their efforts are to be commended, as they surveyed almost 8000 published works, of which 118 remained after screening. Of those remaining, about 1/3rd were of high quality, and the rest were mostly low quality. Yang style Tai Chi Chuan was the most commonly studied lineage, with typical training sessions of half an hour to an hour, twice or three times each week across 12 to 24 weeks. They found that most research studies comprised a majority of female participants from the general community with an average age of 70. From all of these studies, the Brazilian and American researchers extracted outcomes related to 238 measurable effects and 56 associations.

Where are we on the map?

Fogaça and colleagues found evidence that was high quality, suggesting positive effects for "balance, depression, anxiety, cognitive performance, risk of fall, quality of life, well-being, sleep quality, and Parkinson’s disease." The majority of the positive effects are related to holistic psychological effects. The beneficial effects on modulating depression and anxiety and improving sleep quality are particularly notable.

Interestingly, for concentration, agility, muscle mass, HDL cholesterol, stroke, hypertension, and coronary heart disease, there was inconclusive evidence or no effect.

Where are we headed?

Although Tai Chi Chuan was the martial art of focus in the research above, the effects and outcomes are almost certainly widely applicable to many traditional martial arts where mindful practice is embedded in training. The takeaway from this, like so much evidence in individual studies, is that traditional martial arts training represents a form of holistic practice with powerful and widespread health benefits. This extends as well to practices that include many elements found in Tai Chi Chuan with significant self-protection elements, like Okinawan karate, Wing Chun, Aikido, and more.

Something that I often ponder about is this: Are the effects so powerful because living in modern society generally precludes mindful practice? "Trainability" in physiological outcomes like strength usually refers to how strongly a person might respond to a training stimulus and the idea that as you do more training, the effects of dose are lessened. That is, there are diminishing returns over time because the person already has a trained status. Are we so untrained in mindfulness now that these effects are even further enhanced?

Regardless of why the effects are so large, the evidence is compelling that mindfulness should be a key component of training across the lifespan. A relatively convenient methodology exists in the ongoing martial arts classes and training sessions found in just about every community.

item.title: Are You a Collector or Hoarder, or Are You an In-between?
item.description:
Hoarding

Are You a Collector or Hoarder, or Are You an In-between?

Quantity alone cannot distinguish a collector from a hoarder.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • A collectorn and a hoard differ not by volume but by how objects are ordered.
  • Brain science confirms the distinction.
  • In-betweens are not hoarders or collectors.

In 2009, an art installation called Waste Not traveled from Beijing to New York, London, Vancouver, and Sydney. It consisted of ordinary household objects, bottle caps, toothpaste tubes, shoes, and kitchen utensils, all saved over decades by Zhao Xiangyuan, the mother of artist Song Dong. Her son had worried for years that her overstuffed Beijing house was harming her health. Rather than purging her possessions, he sat with her and sorted every item, laying them out in rows grouped by size, color, and use. Not one thing was thrown away. In doing this, something remarkable happened. What had looked like a hoard became a collection, at least in the eyes of museum visitors.

A Pictoral Illustration of Collectors, Hoarders, and Inbetweens
Source: Chat GPT AI

That transformation sits at the heart of a thought-provoking article by anthropologist Katie Kilroy-Marac of the University of Toronto, published in the Journal of Material Culture. Her central question is one I have been curious about throughout my professional life as a collector of Chinese export porcelain. What, exactly, is the difference between a collection and a hoard? And, is there an in-between?

Kilroy-Marac suggests it is not quantity that separates a collector from a hoarder

Most people assume the difference is volume. The hoarder has too much. The DSM-5, the diagnostic manual psychiatrists use, says otherwise. In its Diagnostic Features section for Hoarding Disorder, the manual acknowledges that, in some cases of collecting, the number of possessions may be similar to that accumulated by a person with hoarding disorder. In other words, the sheer number of objects does not, by itself, separate health from pathology.

Then, what does? Kilroy-Marac answers this. She did not rely on impressions. She drew on multiple, independent lines of evidence. For her research, she spent two years as a participant observer with the Toronto Hoarding Coalition, a working group of social workers, public health nurses, fire officials, and cleaning specialists. She conducted 21 semi-structured ethnographic interviews with professional home organizers in the Greater Toronto Area between 2014 and 2015. Also, she analyzed the clinical research that shaped the DSM-5 diagnosis itself, most notably the work of Nordsletten and colleagues, who compared 20 self-identified collectors with 29 people meeting criteria for Hoarding Disorder.

That comparative study found that both groups acquired objects, attached to them, and hesitated to discard them. The collectors, however, were more focused, confining themselves to a narrow range of items, were more selective, planning purchases in advance, and were more likely to organize their possessions, and less likely to accumulate excessively. Roughly 30 percent of the general population collects something, and collecting is generally psychologically beneficial. Hoarding, by contrast, produces disorganized clutter, distress, and impairment in relationships, work, and daily life.

Attentiveness and attachment

Kilroy-Marac distills the distinction into two concepts, thing attentiveness and thing attachment.

Attentiveness is active curation. The collector holds the entire collection in mind at once, knows every item, where it sits, what it means, and what is still missing. The collection is displayed, and most often separate from everyday things. A hoard, on the other hand, is a mass of stuff, which might include newspapers, dust, and debris. It shows no visible sign of intention.

Attachment concerns emotional distance. Collectors are passionate, but they temper that passion. They talk about their objects, share them, trade them, and even brag about them. Hoarders, in the popular and clinical imagination, care too much and not enough at the same time. They are so absorbed in their possessions that the boundary between person and object blurs. Yet, they are unable to maintain or protect what they own. Tellingly, about half the hoarding participants in the Nordsletten study called themselves collectors and could name at least one collection within their hoard. Their diagnosis, however, effectively overruled them because they were unlikely to plan, organize, or share their collections as collectors typically do.

A necessary note of caution

What makes this article worthy of an academic journal, rather than a lifestyle magazine, is that Kilroy-Marac does not stop at the checklist. She asks who gets to draw the line. In the clinical comparison, the collectors were more often men, partnered, educated, and living in larger homes, though this stereotype is changing as more women enter the workplace and have their own resources. Also, Kilroy-Marac’s concept that hoarders are more often women is no longer valid, as a more recent meta-analysis has shown this is not true. Yet, when everyone can accumulate everything, it is no longer the ownership of things that confers collector status. It is how we order them.

Why this matters

Kilroy-Marac’s framework also maps neatly onto what brain science has begun to reveal. The cognitive-behavioral model of hoarding proposed by Frost and Hartl identifies deficits in categorization and decision-making as core features, precisely the sorting failures described. Further, neuroimaging by Tolin and colleagues shows that when people with a hoarding disorder must decide whether to discard a possession, the anterior cingulate cortex and insula, regions that weigh significance and emotional salience, respond abnormally. Every object feels consequential, so nothing can be released. The collector's brain, by contrast, appears to run on Panksepp's SEEKING circuit, the dopaminergic engine of anticipation and pursuit, channeled through focus, selectivity, and the deep pleasure of completing a set. Attentiveness and attachment, it turns out, are not just cultural judgments. They reflect measurably different patterns of neural activity.

And lastly, I believe there is a very small group that are neither collectors nor hoarders but lie somewhere in the middle of the two. This is an area I hope to explore in the future: the in-betweens.

item.title: At What Age Should Your Neurodivergent Child Get a Cell Phone?
item.description:
Parenting

At What Age Should Your Neurodivergent Child Get a Cell Phone?

What's the right age for Fortnite, Roblox, TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube Shorts.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Start with a minimalist or dumb phone at age 10 to 12, then move to a full smartphone between ages 12 and 15.
  • Wait until 15 years old at a minimum for social media for neurodivergent kids.
  • Recognize that online platforms can offer social connection and communication for many neurodivergent youth.
  • Neurodivergent children require active, direct supervision rather than passive restriction or simple delays.

In the United States, 90 percent of kids have a smartphone by the age of 13. Perhaps even more remarkable, 42 percent of them have one by the age of 10. If you don’t like the idea of your 10-year-old having a smartphone that can access anything in the world, you’re not alone. And I’m willing to bet (something that your 10-year-old can do on their phone) that if your 10-year-old doesn’t have a cell phone, they’ve asked you for it repeatedly.

I’ll start with the cell phone because it’s the gateway to most of the other things on the internet. That little magical computer places more computing power in a kid's hand than the astronauts had when they first went to the moon in 1969, and it has only grown more powerful with the arrival of AI chatbots. A decade ago, only about 20 percent of 10-year-olds had smartphones, so their access to other technologies and apps was far less than it is today.

Source: Kelly Sikkema/Unsplash

Kids are growing up in a digital world, and virtually nothing that we do can prevent them from interacting with technology. My two grandsons, not even 18 months old and growing up in homes where their parents have essentially restricted them from watching television, come to visit me with an innate radar for tech. Typically, within two or three minutes, they have found the remote controls for our two televisions and turned them on. They somehow know that this electronic device gets turned on with a push, and they like doing it. These screens beckon to children, even the very young ones, and most kids are fantastic at finding their way to them.

This push, often from the children themselves, for earlier and earlier access to these technologies is a concern. It is particularly problematic for the neurodivergent kids I work with in my clinical practice. It's difficult enough for parents, educators, and providers to manage and harness these digital technologies for typically developing children. But children with ADHD, autism, learning disabilities, and other psychiatric and learning difficulties present a different level of challenge.

What I have come to realize is that simply giving parents an age for when they should allow their neurodivergent children access is probably a poor answer to the wrong question. An age range is useful, and I will give some recommendations at the end of this post. But more importantly, we need to consider the diversity of children and their readiness to use the technology appropriately, or, at the bare minimum, to learn from the times when they don’t.

My instinct to tell parents that their neurodivergent kids should just wait longer for access to technology is understandable, but it's also too simple and sometimes flat-out wrong. For example, there is a fair amount of evidence that some children on the autism spectrum communicate better through the slower, asynchronous back-and-forth of online platforms than they do face-to-face. For these kids, waiting longer would limit their ability to communicate. For kids with ADHD who hyperfocus on Minecraft or Roblox, it may be one of the few places they connect with classmates after school, and they may then be more accepted by them during the school day.

The simplest answer is to restrict them, to keep them away from tech. Unfortunately, that is very hard to do, and it prevents the child from developing the skills they need to interact with others online. Neurodivergent kids need a lot more supervision, an expectation that they will not automatically understand how to interact, and direct training in it. Ultimately, they will live in a world where technology plays an important role, and learning to navigate it has become a new task for good parenting.

Here are some guidelines for determining when your neurodivergent child is ready for a first cell phone and the many other internet-based technologies that come with it.

Cell phones

Minimalist phone: 10 to 12. Smartphone: 12 to 15.
A minimalist or “dumb” phone between 10 and 12 lets a child stay in touch without the dangers of the open internet. A smartphone fits better between 12 and 15, depending on the child’s developmental fit.

Fortnite

13 and up.
Fortnite is rated T for Teen, and 13 and up is our core recommendation. Often, it is the banter around the game, more than the game itself, that is hard for neurodivergent kids. If your 12-year-old’s friends are all playing, you might allow it with your supervision. Before that, Lego Fortnite, rated E10+, is a good substitute.

Roblox

7 or 8 and up, with vigilant supervision of game selection.
Roblox is not a single game but millions of user-generated worlds, some perfectly fine for children and others highly inappropriate. More than anything else here, it demands parental awareness and supervision. With that in place, it can work from as early as age 7 or 8. Unsupervised use is much trickier, and limiting neurodivergent kids until age 12 or 13 may be warranted.

Social media: Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat

15 and up.
These platforms legally require users to be at least 13. Given how sensitive neurodivergent kids can be to them, we recommend 15 and up, which is increasingly the norm in countries outside the United States.

YouTube and YouTube Shorts

8 and up, with controls in place.
Shorts cannot be viewed on YouTube Kids, so they need to be supervised through Google Family Link. When parents use controls that limit the kinds of Shorts, set age ranges, manage time, and turn off the endless-scrolling feed, they can be appropriate for about age 8. Without those controls, Shorts are a real problem for focus and attention in many neurodivergent children.

Ultimately, parents need to use their judgment and understanding of their kids' development. A great rule of thumb is to introduce technologies gradually, making it easier to increase access, but also to take them away if necessary.

item.title: 4 Ways to Become Empowered After a Difficult Childhood
item.description:
Boundaries

4 Ways to Become Empowered After a Difficult Childhood

Living an empowered life starts with self-respect, boundaries, and small choices.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Empowerment begins with self-respect and small actions that honor your boundaries and needs.
  • Developing the ability to say no and align with your own needs can strengthen emotional well-being.
  • Everyday decisions can help create a life that feels more authentic, aligned, and self-directed.

Living an empowered life doesn't mean feeling confident or in control all the time. Instead, it's about agency: knowing you have a voice, choices, and the ability to trust yourself, even when life feels difficult.

For adults raised by high-conflict, controlling, narcissistic, or emotionally invalidating parents, this trust can feel difficult to access. When your needs were minimized, your reality was questioned, or your boundaries were ignored, self-trust needs to be rebuilt through repair; it isn't likely to return through willpower alone.

Early emotional trauma from toxic family dynamics can leave people-pleasing, overexplaining, self-doubt, emotional shutdown, or taking responsibility for everyone else’s feelings. These are not character flaws. They are learned survival responses.

The good news is that learned patterns can change. Personal empowerment begins with awareness and grows through small, self-respecting choices.

1. Empowerment Begins With Awareness, Not Force

Healing does not begin with forcing yourself to be more confident. It begins with noticing your patterns.

For example, when someone grows up under chronic emotional stress, the nervous system may learn to prioritize survival over agency. You may automatically people-please, over-function, shut down, or place other people’s needs ahead of your own. Therefore, personal power begins when you notice these responses without judgment. Awareness creates a pause between an old conditioned reaction and a new choice. It helps you recognize when you are responding to the present and when you are reacting from the past.

Practical tip: For one day, notice the decisions you make. Ask yourself: Is this choice honoring me, or am I acting from fear, obligation, or old conditioning?

2. Reclaim Choice in Small, Everyday Moments

Empowerment is built through small, repeated acts of choice rather than one dramatic decision.

For trauma survivors, personal power can feel risky. Speaking up may once have led to criticism, punishment, rejection, emotional withdrawal, or conflict. Rebuilding agency often needs to happen gradually and safely. Small choices that support empowerment may include:

  • Pausing before responding instead of reacting automatically
  • Saying no without over-explaining
  • Allowing yourself to change your mind
  • Asking for time before making a decision
  • Choosing rest when your body signals exhaustion
  • Expressing a preference without apologizing for it

These choices may seem minor, but they teach your nervous system that autonomy is possible. Over time, these moments build self-trust. You begin to experience yourself as someone who can listen inwardly, make decisions, and respond to your own needs.

Practical tip: Choose one small area of your life this week where you can practice making a choice based on your own preference rather than someone else’s expectation.

3. Boundaries Are Empowerment in Action

Boundaries are not selfish. They are a form of self-respect. Yet they can be especially difficult for people raised in families where boundaries were ignored, criticized, punished, or treated as selfish. If keeping the peace mattered more than your comfort, protecting your time, energy, or emotional well-being may still feel uncomfortable.

Boundaries communicate that your needs matter. It clarifies what you are responsible for and what belongs to someone else.A boundary communicates that your needs, time, energy, and emotional health matter. It helps clarify what you are responsible for and what belongs to someone else. Boundaries can be simple and may sound like:

  • “I am not available for that.”
  • “I need time to think about it.”
  • “That does not work for me.”
  • “I am going to leave this conversation if it becomes disrespectful.”
  • “I cannot take that on right now.”

Guilt often accompanies boundary-setting, especially when you have been conditioned to prioritize other people’s needs. Feeling guilty does not necessarily mean the boundary is wrong. Often, it just means the boundary is new.

Practical tip: Begin with a small boundary. Decline one request without over-apologizing, delay your response rather than answering immediately, or give yourself permission to leave an interaction that feels emotionally draining.

4. Personal Empowerment Is Self-Respect in Action

At its core, personal empowerment means treating yourself as someone who is worthy of care, trust, and respect. It shows up in how you listen to your internal signals, how you speak to yourself under stress, and how you honor your limits.

For those healing from narcissistic, controlling, or emotionally invalidating relationships, empowerment is not about becoming unbreakable. It is about becoming aligned. It may look like speaking honestly, resting without guilt, leaving a harmful dynamic, asking for support, or no longer explaining away behavior that hurts you. Empowerment shows up when you choose self-respect over approval, presence over performance, and authenticity over survival.

Practical tip: Ask yourself, How have I chosen not to betray myself, over approval? When did I choose to be internally aligned, when I was expected to do otherwise: Did I break the pattern?

These choices will not always feel easy. But each one reinforces an important message: My experience matters. My needs matter. I can trust myself.

Building a More Empowered Life

As you practice awareness, make small choices, set boundaries, and repair with compassion, you strengthen your sense of agency. You become a more active participant in your own life rather than feeling defined by old family roles, past conditioning, or other people’s expectations. Healing from a high-conflict childhood, narcissistic parents, or toxic relationships takes time. But you can learn to relate to yourself differently.

You can build self-trust and make choices that honor who you are. You can also create a life that feels increasingly grounded in your own voice, values, and personal power.

Read more about this topic in my book, Adult Children of High Conflict Parents. A version of this article appears on www.drtracyhutchinson.com

item.title: Talk to Your Kids About Your Mortality
item.description:
Parenting

Talk to Your Kids About Your Mortality

How to talk to children about a parent's life-threatening illness.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Angelina Jolie has spoken publicly and often about discussing her serious cancer risk with her kids.
  • Parents worry that sharing their own diagnoses with their kids will exacerbate their children's fears.
  • Honesty, even about a parent's mortality, increases a child's sense of confidence, connection, and security.
  • Reassure your child that they didn't make you sick and that you want them to laugh, play, and have fun.
Source: Omar Lopez/Unsplash

Angelina Jolie has talked publicly about her family history of cancer, including preparing her children for the probability of her relatively young death, which has raised questions for parents about addressing their own health concerns.

Is it healthy to discuss your mortality with your child?

If, like Jolie, you’ve been diagnosed with a potentially fatal condition, it’s a very good idea to talk to your child about what’s happening. You don’t want to tell them too much, but you also don’t want to add extra worries by avoiding or trivializing the situation. How and when you raise the topic matters enormously.

What are the risks and benefits?

The most obvious risk of talking to a child about your mortality is increasing their burden of anxiety and guilt as your condition deteriorates. Try to find a balance where you calmly and lovingly tell them enough, but not too much. After your initial conversation, leave the topic alone. Let them know you’re available to answer their questions, but don’t initiate further discussions unless they show a need for reassurance.

The situation itself is dreadfully unsettling, and you may not be able to allay your child’s fears on your own, so be prepared to get help if that’s needed.

For most families, the benefits of honest conversation outweigh the risks. Somewhat counterintuitively, sharing the truth about hard topics—including your possible death and their life afterward—can increase your child’s sense of connection and security. If you’re able to provide honest reassurance about your reluctant acceptance of the situation, including your deep regrets about leaving them sooner than you’d like, you’ll help your child feel valued, included, and supported.

How can you provide reassurance without alarming your child?

Before talking to your child, get whatever help you need—whether it’s talking to a friend, a partner, or a therapist—in order to provide the calm confidence your child will need when you broach the subject with them. If it helps to have someone with you when you talk to your child, ask that person to be there with you.

Respond to your child’s questions and concerns thoughtfully, lovingly, and honestly. For example, “Yes, this cancer diagnosis is a bad one, and yes, my doctor has told me that I might not make it. I’m going to be in a lot of pain, and I won’t have much energy. But I plan to live until I die, and if there’s a way to beat this, I will. For sure, I love you with my whole heart, and that’s for always.”

After telling your child what’s happening, keep to your normal family routines as much as possible. When that’s impossible, tell your child what changes you’re making and why.

Most importantly, perhaps, do your best to focus on the gifts that each day brings. Make sure your child doesn’t feel guilty about happy experiences, accomplishments, plan-making, laughter, or easy time spent with friends.

What can you expect after you talk to your child?

As your child processes the situation, their emotions will be volatile, as will your own. You might experience anger, tantrums, aggression, or blame. Or you might experience helplessness, clinginess, sleep problems, deep sadness, or despair. As much as possible, respond with calm kindness, both to your child and yourself. Emphasize that all these feelings are normal, and look for ways to express them constructively.

Let friends and family know what you need, and what your child needs. Perhaps some people in your life are toxic just now—too many suggestions, too positive, or too negative. Find ways not to see them. But reach out to those who can give you and your kids some help, comfort, or pleasure, and ask for that help.

This is a seriously challenging experience, so be open to getting professional help for yourself or your child if needed.

At what age should you discuss topics like death?

If you’re dealing with a life-threatening situation right now, this is the time to address the topic, no matter your child’s age. How you address it, however, varies enormously across ages and across individual children’s personalities and needs.

With a young child, keep it simple and practical. Let them know you’re sick, and give them whatever information is relevant for the next little while. For example, “You’ve probably noticed I don’t have much energy these days. I have a medical problem the doctors are trying to help me with, and I’m going to be spending a lot of time in bed for the next little while.”

If your child wants more information, respond briefly and honestly. For example, if your child asks, “When will you get better?” you might say, “I don’t know. I hope I’ll get better soon, but the doctors just don’t know.”

Younger children also need reassurance that they’re not responsible for your health problems. Otherwise, they may worry that their disobedience or other “bad” behavior has made you sick.

How much should you tell them?

If your child asks whether you’re going to die, or what will happen if you don’t get better, be open, honest, and brief. You might say something like, “Yes, sometimes people die from this illness.” Go on to reassure your child that they will be taken care of, giving them the broad specifics of that. For example, “I don’t want to die, but if I do, you and (other family members) will continue to live. You’ll be terribly sad, but you will have each other, and Daddy (or whoever) will take very good care of you.”

Your child might want to know other details about their life after your death. Try to identify the child’s underlying concerns and address only those. Don't provide any unnecessary information they didn't ask about.

The older your child, and the more emotionally mature they are, the more you can share with them about the situation and your own feelings about it, paying attention to their individual questions and needs.

Thank you, Angelina

I’m glad that Angelina Jolie has shared her approach to discussing her significant cancer risk with her kids. It raises some important questions for other parents dealing with this issue, and provides a catalyst for thinking about the answers.
